name: 0.2.0-next.7 regression check against 0.2.0-next.6
host: the private acceptance host: AMD Ryzen 5 3600 (6 cores, 12 threads), 64 GiB, NVMe, Ubuntu 24.04 (Linux 6.8), Node 24.20.0
data: the private consumer seed: 211,205 Firestore documents, 33,352 Storage objects (6.7 GB), one Auth user

candidate.note: the PR #107 head the run used; later commits on the PR change the npm CLI only (MCP timestamp encoding, Windows path display), not the engine

method: One emulator at a time on the otherwise idle host, Firestore, Auth and Storage only unless stated, UI off, plain output.
First start importing the seed: a first start into a new state directory, four per release, alternating.
Resumed start: three restarts on the state each release imported; ready is launch to "All emulators ready".

Writes: ten alternating rounds, each on its own copy of the state next.6 saved, flushed with sync before the start; 2,000 sequential writes each confirmed by a listener, then 4,000 from eight writers at once.

Query shapes: the 26 shapes of docs/benchmarks.md (named as there), 40 iterations each, on resumed data, eight alternating rounds (four per release, in two runs); the figure per shape is the median of the four round medians. Memory: the proportional set size of the whole process tree, in the second run's rounds (two per release), once ready and after the query shapes.
Functions: a project with seven functions (HTTP, Firestore, Storage, schedule and Pub/Sub triggers) and every emulator, five alternating starts per release with no state kept.
Keep data: next.7 only, a project with no seed started four times with --keep-data, 100 documents written per run.
findings: Query shapes, median of four rounds per release: 20 of 26 within 5% of 0.2.0-next.6, two faster (Get one document by id 3.71 to 3.41 ms; == on a boolean, limit 20 18.58 to 17.25 ms) and four slower by 5-20%: Write one document, then delete it 1.69 to 2.02 ms; Collection group, limit 20 18.53 to 20.34 ms; count() with == on a boolean 22.62 to 24.41 ms; Transaction: read, modify, write 3.64 to 3.83 ms. On those four shapes 0.2.0-next.6 spread by 16-61% between its own rounds and 0.2.0-next.7 by 3-5%, and every 0.2.0-next.7 round lies inside the range of 0.2.0-next.6 but one (Collection group, 20.71 ms against its highest 20.61 ms). Only the write touches code next.7 changed (a check for timestamps finer than a microsecond); the 2,000-write lane, the stronger measure of a write, is unchanged.
Memory is 11 MB higher once ready (0.159 against 0.148 GiB) and 21 MB higher after the query shapes (0.266 against 0.245 GiB), in both rounds.

A start on a freshly copied state directory took 0.65-16 s on both releases (most often several seconds) until the copy was flushed with sync, then 0.56-0.66 s on both: the slow start the next.6 benchmark noted on copied state is the copy's pending writes reaching the disk, not the engine.
